title: The Nihang dals
hookLine: blue-clad orders keeping the martial traditions and their own customs

lines: A KETTLE DRUM, SLOW AND HEAVY.
A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.
cards: You hear it before you see anything: a big kettle drum, struck slow and heavy, carried on horseback or on a cart at the head of a line. Behind it, a tall triangular flag on a pole.
Behind the flag, riders and walkers in deep blue, steel at their belts and in their turbans. Year one met the Nihangs at Hola Mohalla, and year three met the elders' army they trace themselves to.
Today is the procession itself, and what it's announcing.

teach.b: A dal is an army, a host, a band that moves together. The Nihang dals are the orders of Nihangs, each with its own leader, camps and customs, and each keeping the martial life of the old Khalsa riders.
There is more than one, and they don't all do everything the same way. The drum is the nagara, and in a Nihang procession it goes in front.
Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum, and that beating it was a way of saying: this is a sovereign people, and it is here.
When a Nihang dal moves today, the nagara still goes first. A salok of Bhagat Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the drum a meaning.

teach.h: KABIR: THE DRUM BEATS IN THE MIND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the drum beats in the sky of the mind, and the aim is struck.

teach.h: A HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.
teach.b: The true hero is the one who fights for deen, who may be cut apart piece by piece and still never leaves the field. Deen is a word some readers render as the faith, and some as the helpless.
The drum is inside first; the battle is first a battle of the mind; and the hero stays, whatever it costs.

That's what the blue army says it keeps: the outward life of the old riders, horses, weapons, the drum, and the inward reason for it. Some Nihang customs differ from the code you read in the last block.
Sikhs hold a range of views about that, and some honor the dals as living memory of the Khalsa's hardest years. This path describes what they keep, and leaves the rest to the panth.

how: Nihang dals process with the nagara drum and the Nishan Sahib flag in front, notably at festivals such as Hola Mohalla, and keep horses, weapons training and their own customs in their camps.

o: village councils that settle Sikh disputes
blue-clad orders keeping the old riders' life
volunteer kitchens that feed a festival crowd

s: there is only one Nihang dal, and all do things the same way
there is more than one, each with its own leader, camps and customs.
in Kabir's salok, the hero never leaves the field

the nagara marches at the back of a procession

games.q: Kabir's salok opens with a drum. where does it beat first?
o: at the head of a procession.
in the sky of the mind.
at the gate of a fort.
games.why: the drum beats in the sky of the mind: the battle is inward before it is outward.

practice: Let your breath fall into the slow beat of the nagara: in, two, three; out, two, three. With each out-breath, picture the drum sounding first inside, in the sky of the mind.
Then hold one person who can't easily stand up for themselves steady in mind while the drum keeps time.
